newsitem.title: CHINA: China central banker sees bank reform as priority.
newsitem.headline: China central banker sees bank reform as priority.

text.p: China's central bank governor Dai Xianglong said on Thursday that tackling modernisation of state banks burdened with huge bad debts would top his agenda in the next few years.
However, he ruled out an interest rate cut or easing of credit to help state firms struggling to repay their loans.
"We should... bring the operation of all state commercial banks in line with international practice by the end of the century," Dai told a news conference.
The People's Bank of China plans to allow more state enterprises to raise funds through bond issues to reduce the burden on state banks and the reliance of industries on bank loans, Dai said.
He gave no details of the planned expansion in bond issues.
State banks provide about 80 percent of operational funds needed by domestic enterprises, but have been grappling in recent years with ever rising unpaid loans held by the lumbering state sector.

"The state banks should strictly bring their loan portfolios under control and concretely improve cash management," Dai said, adding that efficient state firms would continue to have access to credit.

An estimated 70 percent of China's 100,000 state enterprises are operating in the red after being forced to sink or swim in a market economy created by China's decision nearly two decades ago to dump Stalinist central planning and embrace reforms.

Unpaid interest owed to state bank on loans in arrears of up to two years totalled 143.1 billion yuan ($17.2 billion) at the end of June, up 24.6 billion yuan, or 20.76 percent, from the start of the year, Dai said.
China would set aside 30-40 billion yuan each year to write off bad debts owed by state firms to state banks. It set aside 30 billion yuan for this purpose in 1997.
Dai gave no details of the size of China's non-performing and bad loans.
However, he said he saw no need to cut interest rates or ease a credit squeeze enforced to curb galloping inflation.
"We believe the current rate is still appropriate," he said.
Current actual interest rates after taking inflation into account were about 4.0 percent, he said. Analysts say the rates were the lowest since 1990.
China cut interest rates twice last year, easing a three-year-old credit squeeze but has since said repeatedly that it will retain an "appropriately tight" monetary policy.
"The financial sector remains committed in 1997 to pursuing the moderately tight monetary policy, safeguarding and mitigating financial risk," Dai said.
But many analysts in Hong Kong expect China to ease credit this year because inflation has cooled in recent years.

"Three years (of credit squeeze) is long enough and inflation has fallen below the government target. More importantly, a lot of state owned enterprises are having difficulties," said Qu Hongbin, a Hong Kong-based economist with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"The government may want to ease credit to make life easier for state owned enterprises... and improve the efficiency of the economy," Qu said.
Governor Dai vowed to intensify a crackdown on irregularities among financial institutions to avoid a crisis similar to the one that has battered Thailand.
The central bank would intensify supervision and regulation of financial institutions, some of which are illegal, charge exorbitant interest rates or falsify their accounts, he said.
China's thousands of small credit cooperatives would be streamlined, merging them into larger financial institutions or dissolving them, Dai said.
